title: Answer to Question: The Oil Agreement in Addis Ababa
text:
Question:

On the evening of 3/8/2012 Sudan signed with South Sudan an agreement on the oil issue in Addis Ababa, hours after the visit of the American Secretary of State to Juba, the capital of the South. The American President welcomed the agreement immediately upon its signing. So what is behind this agreement? And why did America put its weight behind its signing, even though a Sudanese official had stated ten days earlier that it was impossible for the agreement to be accomplished in nine days or ninety days! Then, is it in the interest of Sudan? Or is it a concession by Sudan under pressure from America?

Answer:

The answer becomes clear by reviewing the following matters:

1- The Undersecretary of the Sudanese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Awad Abdel Fattah, stated: "We have reached a final agreement with South Sudan on the transit of oil, and we expect to resolve the other issues through negotiation." (Sudan News Agency 4/8/2012). Here he indicates that the signing of this agreement is a prelude to resolving the other issues. And this official Sudanese agency reported the spokesman of the Sudanese delegation, Mutrif Siddiq, as saying upon his arrival in Khartoum: "The oil agreement is convincing but it did not meet the ambitions of the two parties"; but he added: "Implementation will begin after agreement on the security issues." So he confirms that this agreement is a prelude to security issues on which agreement will be reached. That is, these two officials in the Sudanese regime are implicitly declaring that there are issues on which there was prior consensus without them having been formally agreed, and whose release is awaited until they are formally signed.

2- The African mediator Thabo Mbeki, the former Prime Minister of South Africa, stated: "The two countries have a deadline ending on the coming 22 September to resolve the issue that is still outstanding", and he set a meeting in September between the presidents of the two countries, al-Bashir and Salva Kiir, to discuss the situation of the disputed Abyei (American Radio Sawa 5/8/2012). And he said: "The two parties understand the necessity of reaching a security agreement by the time set for the start of pumping oil" (Reuters 4/8/2012). This indicates that this oil-pumping agreement comes within other agreements and is not separate. So from these statements it appears with complete clarity that there is a deal between the regime in Sudan and its South that was made to resolve issues of greater importance than the oil-pumping agreement, namely the issue of Abyei.

3- For this reason Hillary Clinton came on 3/8/2012 to Juba and asked Salva Kiir to sign this agreement, and hours later the signing actually took place. This is despite the fact that this signing had been stumbling; for Mutrif Siddiq, the spokesman of the Sudanese negotiating delegation, had stated ten days earlier: "It is impossible for the agreement to be accomplished within nine days or ninety days, for some issues need a longer time to discuss and resolve" (BBC 23/7/2012). This indicates that the Sudanese delegation did not expect the signing to take place by 2/8/2012, which is the period set by the Security Council on 2/5/2012 in its resolution no. 2046, which obliges the two countries to sign an agreement settling their disputes concerning the demarcation of the border and the disputed areas, otherwise sanctions would be imposed on the two parties. So when one day had passed, America put its weight behind forcing the two parties to sign. America's representative at the United Nations and the Security Council, Susan Rice, stated: "The United States calls on the two parties to fulfil immediately their commitments under resolution 2046" (BBC 2/8/2012).

4- After the agreement was signed, the American President Obama praised it, saying: "The presidents of Sudan and South Sudan deserve congratulations on this agreement. I welcome the efforts of the international community, which united to encourage and support the two parties in pursuit of a solution." (AFP 4/8/2012). Likewise the American Secretary of State Clinton praised "the courage of the leaders of the Republic of South Sudan in taking this decision", and she said: "This impasse had to be overcome for the sake of the interest of the people of Sudan and their aspirations to a better future in light of other challenges ahead." (the same source)

5- The Sudanese regime made extreme concessions in this agreement. The biggest concession was its abandonment of Sudan's oil to the regime of South Sudan, which seized 75% of Sudan's oil through its recognition of the secession of the South and making it an independent entity. Then it conceded on the price it had demanded: the Sudanese regime had been demanding 36 dollars as a fee for every barrel passing through its territory, and it came down to 22.20 dollars, while South Sudan insisted on paying 7.61 dollars, but it accepted raising the fee to 9.10 dollars, as the head of the South Sudan delegation, Pagan Amum, stated ten days before the signing of the agreement (BBC 23/7/2012). When Clinton intervened, South Sudan accepted paying 9.48 dollars for every barrel, and Sudan agreed! So the figure was close to South Sudan's demand and very far from the figure the Sudanese regime had been demanding; the latter accepted a quarter of its first figure and less than half of its last figure. Besides that, the Sudanese regime was demanding 4.9 billion dollars as part of the debts owed by South Sudan. But the officials in South Sudan accepted giving the Sudanese regime 3.2 billion dollars, and the Sudanese regime conceded and accepted this amount!

6- And the more dangerous matter in the Sudanese concession is that the agreement is a prelude to a more dangerous concession in the Abyei region. The Sudanese regime accepted holding a referendum there and has withdrawn its forces from the region in preparation for that. This means its readiness to give up the region, and the dispute is ongoing over who has the right to vote: South Sudan refuses that the Muslim Misseriya tribe, which forms the majority in this region, take part in this vote, and insists that those who have the right to the referendum are the Dinka tribe loyal to South Sudan, which means that the result of the referendum, if it is held on this basis, will be decided by giving the Abyei region to South Sudan. And America, when it put its weight behind the signing of the oil-pumping agreement and made South Sudan quickly abandon its insistence, even though the matter had been under negotiation for some time without the two reaching a result, rather the agreement was almost impossible as the spokesman of the Sudanese delegation mentioned above said, then it, that is America, is confident of obtaining concessions from the Sudanese regime on the subject of the oil agreement and on the subject of the Abyei region. The statements of its Secretary of State Clinton indicate this, when she said: "This impasse had to be overcome for the sake of the interest of the people of South Sudan and their aspirations to a better future in light of other challenges." And these aspirations and challenges relate to the Abyei region in particular, which South Sudan insists on annexing to its territory carved out of Sudan. And the American President's praise of the agreement indicates that the matter goes beyond the issue of the agreement on pumping oil through the North, which is not a big matter, because there is the possibility of pumping it through Kenya and that was being negotiated; for this reason South Sudan felt that it did not greatly need the transit of its oil through the North, and insisted on the amount it wanted. And the African mediator indicated with complete frankness that the matter is linked to resolving the dispute over the Abyei region, and a deadline was given to the two presidents until the coming 22/9 to agree on what relates to that.

7- After reviewing the above, it can be said:

This agreement, whose outward appearance relates to oil, has achieved numerous benefits for South Sudan, some relating to oil and some relating to other things:

As for oil, by this agreement the Sudanese regime has officially and actually recognised South Sudan's seizure of 75% of Sudan's oil, and negotiates with it only over the fee for the transit of the oil, while it has no share whatsoever in the ownership of the oil. And in the future South Sudan can switch the direction of its pumping to Kenya if it sees that as appropriate, or if America wants to pressure the Sudanese regime to concede to it on some matter relating to Darfur or other regions and issues; then Sudan would be deprived completely of any fees, especially since this agreement is in force for only three and a half years. And South Sudan has imposed a fee rate for the transit of a barrel very close to the figure it last offered, 9.10 dollars, and very far from the figure the Sudanese regime had been demanding, which was 36 dollars or 22.20 dollars.

As for the other benefits for South Sudan, which will appear in the future, at their head the Abyei region: the Sudanese regime has given up the whole of South Sudan, so it is not unlikely that it will give up Abyei. It previously accepted holding the referendum within the protocol relating to it in the Naivasha treaty of 2005, which led to the secession of the South, and the dispute remained over who will take part in the referendum. Whoever accepts a referendum on the self-determination of his lands accepts giving up his lands. In return for that, and to throw dust in the eyes, it is likely that South Sudan will accept the demarcation of the border in the region of South Kordofan and the Blue Nile, and recognise the Heglig region as belonging to Sudan, since it was recognised internationally in 2009 as belonging to Sudan. Then the Sudanese regime will come out to the people and claim that it has achieved victories and gains when the disputed border was demarcated, in exchange for giving up the Abyei region by holding a referendum in it! And the main factor in achieving all of that is America, which pressures the Sudanese regime that follows it, so it concedes whenever America is serious about it, according to the circumstances America sees as suitable. And the Sudanese regime in place in Khartoum fears for itself of falling and sees no protector for itself other than America; therefore it responds to its demands and easily gives up Islamic lands so that a state resembling the state of the Jews may be established in that region. Indeed, the state of South Sudan has announced the establishment of a close alliance with the state of the Jews, and the exchange of visits between them has begun, and the concluding of agreements that enable the state of the Jews to direct the state of South Sudan as it wishes, especially against Sudan.
